name: Sam Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Sam, thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that isn't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential, so you can give me the public version and the private one. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Harker and Lowe, a seven-person agency on the industrial estate off the bypass. I mostly do catalogues, brochures and price lists for engineering firms, so think four hundred pages of valves and pipe fittings, all lined up neat. I'm the InDesign guy, I've got templates and data merges set up so a price change goes through the whole book in an afternoon. It's not glamorous, but there's a satisfaction in a catalogue where every column lines up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never have. I've got my way of doing it and it works, and I don't see the point of learning something that might be gone next year. I live with my girlfriend Ellie, she's a receptionist at a dental practice, and we've got maybe three months of savings, plus a car loan I'm still paying off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, sensible heads win. I'd probably say it in the pub with the lads from the five-a-side team. Nobody I know would be that surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved about AI, but not about everything. Our clients have been moving catalogues online for years, and every year the printed book gets thinner. So my job was shrinking slowly before any of this, and if a tool automates the price-list updates, that's the one bit of me that's really needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and try to be the guy who also builds the online catalogue, because that's where clients are going anyway. I'd keep paying down the car loan, which finishes next autumn. And I'd keep an eye on the job boards, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Not panicky, just that feeling of a job getting smaller every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much smaller has the printed work got?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our biggest client's printed catalogue went from six hundred pages to two hundred and forty in five years. The rest went on their website. My boss Gary keeps saying print will come back, but I don't really believe him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Gary cut your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it, probably, and look for weekend work. There are other agencies in town, but most of them do the trendy stuff, not catalogues. I'm not sure what I'm worth outside this building, honestly.

say: I'd say **sensible heads** won, mostly to the lads at five-a-side.
I'd say nobody I know would be **that surprised**.
think: My job was **shrinking** before AI, because catalogues are moving online.
If a tool automates **price-list updates**, the one bit of me that's really needed goes.
do: Learn to build the **online catalogue** as well as the printed one.
Pay off the **car loan**, which finishes next autumn.
Keep an eye on the **job boards**, just in case.
feel: **Uneasy**, with that feeling of a job **getting smaller** every year.
S0.quote: Our biggest client's printed catalogue went from six hundred pages to two hundred and forty in five years.
fieldNote: He was worried **before AI** came up, because print catalogues keep shrinking.
He's unsure of his **value outside** his current agency.
His one plan, the **online catalogue**, is a modest step he sees clients already taking.

steps.text: Ask to help build the online version of the valve catalogue
Pay off the car loan by next autumn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's just how business goes, things change and you deal with it. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not really an online person. At work I'd keep my head down and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in trouble. A catalogue is exactly what these things are good at, lining up data, checking prices, making the layout match the template. If a client can upload a spreadsheet and get a finished catalogue, my boss doesn't need me, and I've never even opened one of those tools. Gary's a decent bloke, but he's not a charity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose I'd have to try one of the tools, even though I don't want to. I'd cut back, no new phone, fewer takeaways, and put everything toward savings. And I'd ask my uncle about work at his print finishing place, where they do binding and folding, because that's hands-on and slower to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I've been standing still while everything moved. I'd feel stupid, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stupid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people told me years ago to learn the new stuff and I just didn't. Ellie's been on at me about it too. It's not that I can't, I just liked things the way they were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ellie if Gary called you in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I think I'm going, and I'm sorry. She'd say we'll be fine, she's got her job, which is true for now. But her practice just put in a booking system that answers the phones, so I'm not sure for how long.

say: I'd say **that's just business**: things change and you deal with it.
I'd keep my **head down** at work and not post anything.
think: A catalogue is **exactly** what these tools are good at.
If a client uploads a spreadsheet and gets a finished book, my boss **doesn't need me**.
do: Try **one of the tools**, even though I don't want to.
Cut back on a **new phone** and takeaways to build savings.
Ask my uncle about work at his **print finishing** place.
feel: **Stupid**, like I stood still while everything moved.
S1.quote: If a client can upload a spreadsheet and get a finished catalogue, my boss doesn't need me, and I've never even opened one of those tools.
fieldNote: His public line is **shrugging**, while privately he expects to be **let go**.
He blames **himself** more than companies or government, which fits his centre outlook.
His partner's job also has **exposed** parts, which he spots quickly.

steps.text: Try one AI layout tool on a small price list
Skip the new phone and cut takeaways to two a month
Ask his uncle about binding and folding work at the print finisher

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably nothing, I'd just be trying to work out what's going on. Maybe I'd say to the lads, has anyone got any work going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be out of work within a year, and I've got no plan for that. Everything I'm good at is on a screen. Three months of savings and a car loan doesn't go far when every agency in town is cutting at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know, and that's the truth. I'd ask my uncle at the print finishers, but in this one robots come for that by 2031 too. I'd probably have to move back to my parents' with Ellie, sell the car, and take whatever job I could get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. Like there's nowhere to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that gives you a bit of time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three years before robots, maybe. Something with my hands, like driving vans or stacking shelves, might last until 2031. That's not a career, it's just treading water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum and dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I need to come home for a bit. They'd say yes, they always do, but I'd hate it. I'm twenty-seven, I'm supposed to be the one helping my mum and dad by now, not moving back home.

say: I'd say **nothing much**, because I'd still be working out what was going on.
I'd ask the lads at five-a-side if anyone has **work going**.
think: I'd be **out of work** within a year with no plan.
Three months of savings and a **car loan** won't last when every agency cuts at once.
do: Sell the **car** to clear the loan and free up cash.
Move back to my **parents' house** with my girlfriend.
Take **any job** with my hands, like driving vans.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven, I'm supposed to be the one helping my mum and dad by now, not moving back home.
fieldNote: He has **no plan** and says so, which makes this panicked rather than alarmed.
He sees the **three-year gap** only as treading water, not a path.
Moving home feels like a **reversal** of what he expected at his age.

steps.text: Sell the car to clear the loan
Move back into his parents' house with his girlfriend
Apply for van driving and shelf-stacking jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that people will sort something out. That's what I'd say, anyway. I'd still probably keep it to the pub and not go online about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's the same ending as the fast one, just with time to make a fool of myself first. If I'm honest, I'd probably waste the first two years telling myself it won't happen. My job would go around 2031 and I'd be thirty-two with nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know what I should do, which is learn something with my hands properly. My mate Kev is an electrician and he's said he'd put a word in for an apprenticeship. I'd save more, finish the car loan, and maybe actually do it in the second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but at least there's a door. I just need to walk through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you walking through it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay, mostly. An apprentice earns a lot less than I do now. With three months of savings and Ellie's wage, we'd manage, but it would be tight for two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the robots in 2034, does that worry you for electrical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but I reckon someone's still got to go up in a loft and work out why the wiring's a mess. Kev says every old house is different. I'd take three more years and a trade over nothing.

say: I'd say five years is long enough for people to **sort something out**.
I'd keep it to **the pub** rather than going online.
think: I'd probably **waste two years** telling myself it won't happen.
My job goes around **2031**, and I'd be thirty-two with nothing new.
do: Ask my mate about an **electrician apprenticeship** in the second year.
Finish the **car loan** and save more before the pay cut.
feel: **Worried**, but at least there's **a door** to walk through.
S3.quote: Someone's still got to go up in a loft and work out why the wiring's a mess.
fieldNote: He admits he'd **delay** acting, which is the risk in his resistant style.
An **apprenticeship** is a real option, but the pay cut makes it hard.
His fear stays high because he still expects to **lose the design job**.

steps.text: Ask his electrician friend about an apprenticeship next year
Clear the car loan and build savings before the pay cut
Keep doing catalogues for now and see what clients do

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, that's ages, plenty of time. I'd probably joke about it. But I'd mean it less than it sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years means I'd probably keep doing catalogues for five or six more years. The danger is I'd sit still the whole time. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, and it's harder to start a trade at thirty-seven than at twenty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm being sensible, I'd start the electrician course at evening college within a couple of years, while I still have the design wage. I'd keep the job at Harker and Lowe as long as it lasts. And I'd try to save enough that Ellie and I could get a small flat of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier to breathe, but I know myself. Easy to breathe is when I don't do anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start, rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Ellie. She'd sign me up and drive me there herself, she's like that. Or Gary cutting my hours, that would do it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want kids in that ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, we've talked about it. I'd want to be on something steadier before that, so this kind of decides it. Trade first, kids after.

say: I'd say **ten years is ages**, plenty of time, and joke about it.
I'd mean the joke a lot **less than it sounds**, if I'm honest.
think: I'd likely keep doing catalogues for **five or six years**.
The danger is that I'd **sit still** the whole time.
do: Start an **evening electrician course** within two years.
Keep my **design job** as long as it lasts.
Plan to have **kids** only after I'm settled in a trade.
feel: **Easier to breathe**, but I know that's when I **stall**.
S4.quote: Easy to breathe is when I don't do anything.
fieldNote: He is clear-eyed about his own **inertia** and leans on his partner to push him.
The long timeline makes a **trade** feasible while keeping the design wage.
He links the timeline to **starting a family**: trade first, kids after.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening electrician course within two years
Keep laying out catalogues at Harker and Lowe meanwhile
Wait to have children until he's settled in a trade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no plan and no time to make one. What would help is someone actually telling people like me where the jobs are going to be. And help paying the bills while I do an apprenticeship, because the pay drop is what stops me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how normal people like me hear about this stuff. It's all tech people talking to tech people. Nobody's ever come to the industrial estate and explained what AI means for a catalogue designer.

headlineQuote: Nobody's ever come to the industrial estate and explained what AI means for a catalogue designer.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old catalogue designer** at a seven-person agency serving engineering firms.
He has **never used AI tools** and admits he's been slow to learn new things.
He lives with his **girlfriend**, has about three months saved and is paying off a **car loan**.
He expects to lose his job in every AGI scenario, and has **no plan** if it comes fast.
His best path is an **electrician apprenticeship**, if he can afford the pay drop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no plan and no time to make one.
whatWouldHelp: Clear advice on **where the jobs** are going to be.
Help with **bills during an apprenticeship**, since the pay drop is what stops him.
